prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: She, Butterworth, Gorgeous

outputs.L1:
She said the cornflake cake made her day. She said a man cannot be blamed for being unfaithful: his heart is not in tune with his extremities, and it is simply the nature of his body chemistry. She said all sorts of things.

We saw a duck pond and a man with a tub of maggots and a tub of sweetcorn. We saw the walled garden and the old-fashioned library in the park, then stopped for a cup of tea in a café, where we had the cornflake cake cut into halves with the handle of a plastic fork. We saw yellow crocuses growing in a ring around a naked tree, the sky showing in purple triangles between the branches.

We looked in the window of Butterworth’s at the bikes: they were beautiful, all of them.

“Gorgeous,” she said.

The sun was pushing through the iced air and landing on us—on our heads and our shoulders and the backs of our legs. We bought nail varnish remover from Wilko’s, a bath sheet, and two Diet Cokes.

She said she had been talking to Jesus and God because she did not want to go to hell, although, as she said, correctly, we had been through hell already, hadn’t we? She said a woman should know her place, should wait.

She lit a cigarette.
outputs.L2:
She told me the cornflake cake had brightened her whole day. She also said a man shouldn’t be held responsible for cheating, because his feelings don’t line up with the rest of his body, and that this is simply how his chemistry works. She said many other things too.

We passed a duck pond, and there was a man carrying one container of maggots and another of sweetcorn. In the park, we visited the walled garden and the old-style library, then paused at a café for tea. There, we split the cornflake cake in two using the handle of a plastic fork.

We noticed yellow crocuses arranged in a circle around a bare tree, with pieces of sky showing through the branches like purple triangles. At Butterworth’s, we stood at the window admiring the bicycles; every one of them looked lovely. “Gorgeous,” she said.

The sun broke through the freezing air and settled on our heads, our shoulders, and the backs of our legs. We went to Wilko’s and bought nail polish remover, a bath sheet, and two Diet Cokes.

She said she had been speaking to Jesus and to God because she didn’t want to end up in hell, though, as she rightly pointed out, we had already been through hell, hadn’t we. She said a woman ought to understand her position and be patient. Then she lit a cigarette.
outputs.L3:
She enjoyed the cornflake cake very much and said that it had made her day. The small treat seemed to lift her spirits, giving the moment a sense of warmth and simple pleasure.

During their conversation, she expressed strong views about relationships and the roles of men and women. She spoke about men’s unfaithfulness, suggesting that it was something women often had to endure. She also talked about women knowing their place and the importance of waiting, revealing beliefs shaped by experience, patience, and perhaps disappointment.

They walked together through the park, taking in the sights around them. They passed a duck pond, a walled garden, and an old-fashioned library. Crocuses were beginning to bloom, adding colour to the surroundings, and they noticed bicycles displayed in a shop window. The walk gave them time to talk, observe, and share a quiet stretch of the day.

Later, they stopped at a café, where they had tea and cake together. Afterwards, they went shopping and bought nail varnish remover, a bath sheet, and two Diet Cokes. These ordinary errands sat alongside the more personal and reflective parts of their conversation, making the day feel both everyday and meaningful.

She also spoke about her faith and fears. She said that she talked to Jesus and God because she was afraid of hell. At the same time, she observed that they had already been through hell, suggesting that their past experiences had been so painful that they felt like a kind of suffering in themselves.
outputs.L4:
The passage follows a day spent in the company of a woman whose ordinary conversation gradually reveals a complicated inner life. At first, the scene appears simple and casual: the speaker observes small details of the outing, the places they pass through, the things they eat, see, touch, and notice. The writing lingers on sensory impressions—colors, smells, textures, sounds, and fragments of movement—so that everyday objects and public spaces feel vivid and immediate. Shops, streets, food, clothing, religious images, and passing remarks all become part of the emotional landscape.

As the day unfolds, however, the woman’s casual comments begin to carry deeper meaning. What may seem at first like light conversation reveals her beliefs about love, gender roles, religion, suffering, and endurance. She speaks in ways that suggest she has absorbed painful ideas about what women should accept, how love should feel, and how suffering can be justified or made meaningful. Her remarks show how personal pain is often shaped by larger social and religious expectations. The passage does not present these ideas through direct argument; instead, it allows them to emerge through small moments, unfinished observations, and fragments of dialogue.

A central effect of the passage is the contrast between pleasure and hardship. The day contains moments of enjoyment: the pleasure of being outside, of noticing beautiful or curious things, of sharing food or conversation, of moving through ordinary places. Yet these pleasures are repeatedly shadowed by signs of difficulty. Beneath the surface of the outing are hints of emotional damage, social pressure, poverty, loneliness, or resignation. The woman’s experiences seem to have taught her to accept pain as normal, perhaps even as something connected to love, duty, or faith.

The style of the passage reinforces this tension. Rather than offering a smooth, straightforward narrative, it is built from vivid details and broken impressions. This fragmented structure mirrors the way meaning often appears in real life: not as a clear explanation, but through gestures, comments, objects, and memories. Ordinary things become charged with significance because they are connected to the woman’s unspoken history and to the social world that has shaped her.

Overall, the passage suggests that everyday moments are never merely ordinary. A simple day out can reveal deep emotional truths and expose the hidden pressures that influence how people understand themselves and their relationships. By placing small pleasures beside signs of suffering, the passage shows how beauty, pain, faith, and social expectation can exist side by side in daily life. Its power lies in making the reader feel that even the most casual remarks and familiar objects can contain a much larger story.
outputs.L5:
She arrived in Butterworth just as the evening light turned the streets gold. There was something quiet and graceful about the town, a calm rhythm in the air that made every step feel meaningful. She walked past the old shops and the busy roads, noticing how ordinary moments could become beautiful when seen with the right heart.

To her, Butterworth was more than a place on a map. It was a memory waiting to be made, a story unfolding with every smile, every passing breeze, and every glowing sunset over the horizon. She felt peaceful there, as if the town had welcomed her gently.

And in that moment, standing beneath the soft sky, she looked absolutely gorgeous—not only because of how she appeared, but because of the happiness shining through her.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary prose poem in a single paragraph about two women spending an afternoon in a small English town, mixing mundane errands with unsettling remarks about faith, gender, and relationships.
counterfactuals.output: They spend the afternoon in a small English town where the rain has forgotten its purpose and hangs about in the air like a rumour, going first to the chemist for antihistamines and a lipstick the colour of dried cherries, then to the post office to send a parcel to a man neither of them wants to name, and all the while the church bell keeps trying the hour again as if practice might make it true. In the queue, one says she no longer believes in God but still feels watched when she eats meat on a Friday; the other says belief is mostly a question of who is allowed to be forgiven before tea. Outside, schoolgirls in pleated skirts smoke behind the charity shop, bright and bored as match flames, and an old man in a mobility scooter calls them angels with a look that makes the word go sour. They buy batteries, plums, bin liners, a sympathy card, and because the high street is short and cannot keep a secret, they pass the same bridal boutique three times, its window full of women without heads wearing gowns white enough to be accused. One laughs and says marriage is a room you enter because everyone insists there is a garden on the other side; the other says she has always preferred doors that lock from within. At the café, where the waitress has blue nails and the patience of a minor saint, they share a pot of tea and a slice of something vegan and dense, speaking of mothers, lovers, rent, blood tests, the new vicar with the handsome tired face, the way men say “calm down” as if naming a weather system they invented. A dog tied outside the butcher’s begins to howl, not sadly but with conviction, and for a moment all the shoppers turn, holding their paper bags and prescriptions, their cheap umbrellas and private verdicts, as if an oracle has opened its mouth between the sausages and the cash machine. Then the rain strengthens, the buses sigh at the kerb, and the two women walk home under one umbrella that is not wide enough for either of them, their shoulders touching and not touching, their laughter rising oddly in the wet street, like hymns sung by people who know the words are dangerous and sing them anyway.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary vignette in the style of modern British observational fiction, with vivid sensory details, odd dialogue, and no clear plot, centered on cornflake cake, a park, shops, and a woman saying contradictory things.
counterfactuals.output:
The cornflake cake sat in its paper case like a small act of civic neglect.

It had been made, Denise said, by one of the Brownies, though she also said Brownies had been discontinued due to safeguarding, and anyway no child could produce chocolate with that particular sheen, that dull institutional gloss like the top of a municipal piano. She held it in the flat of her hand as we crossed the road by the chemist, where an A-board advertised flu jabs, ear syringing, and a “luxury gifting range” of lavender soaps.

“I never eat sweet things,” Denise said, biting into it. “They make me feel absolutely myself.”

A number 43 bus exhaled at the stop. The driver looked straight ahead with the expression of a man remembering a saucepan left on. Outside the charity shop, three headless mannequins wore sequinned tops in shades of bruised fruit. There was a card in the window: DOG WALKER — DISCREET. Next door, the halal butcher had arranged lamb ribs in the window with a tenderness that seemed almost floral.

The park gates were painted green, or had once been. Now they were the colour of old spinach and rain. Inside, the path shone with a recent shower. Wet leaves stuck to the tarmac in the shapes of countries no one had invaded yet. A crow stood on the back of a bench and shouted something unhelpful.

Denise put the remaining half of the cornflake cake into her coat pocket.

“You’ll ruin the lining,” I said.

“I haven’t got a lining,” she said. “This coat is entirely theoretical.”

It was a beige coat, heavy and belted, with enormous buttons like boiled sweets. She had bought it, she told me, from a shop that wasn’t there anymore, except that it was still there, only under different management and selling phone cases and devotional candles. Denise said she hated nostalgia, then described at length the Woolworths pick-and-mix: the pink shrimps, the white mice, the cola bottles furred with sugar like archaeological finds.

By the bandstand, two boys were kicking a flat football. Each kick made a papery clack. A woman with a dachshund stood beneath a plane tree saying, “Monty, don’t be political,” while Monty worried a crisp packet with the quiet determination of a solicitor.

The air smelled of damp bark, fryer oil from the parade, and that metallic smell pigeons give off when they gather in numbers. In the little kiosk near the pond, a man in fingerless gloves was selling tea, coffee, hot chocolate, and, according to a handwritten sign, “soup (soup varies).” Denise read this aloud twice.

“Soup varies,” she said. “That’s the truest thing I’ve ever seen. I don’t believe in truth.”

We sat on a bench dedicated to Brian, who had loved this park, his family, and steam railways. The dedication had been scratched at with a key, so that Brian now appeared to have loved “this ark” and “team ailways,” which seemed more private and profound.

Denise took the cornflake cake out of her pocket. It had gathered a lining of beige fluff after all.

“I thought you didn’t have a lining,” I said.

“That’s not lining,” she said. “That’s evidence.”

She ate it anyway, slowly, picking threads from the chocolate with the concentration of a surgeon. A little girl in a silver puffer coat came past on a scooter and stared at us as if we were furniture she had not approved.

From the high street came the muffled percussion of commerce: shutters rattling, a delivery cage clanging over paving stones, someone laughing outside the betting shop with a sound like a tray dropped in a canteen. The shops were all lit too brightly against the afternoon. The bakery had iced buns in the window, each with a red cherry pressed into it like an alarm button. The nail bar glowed pink and empty. In the mini-market, pyramids of oranges leaned against pyramids of loo roll, and a handwritten sign over the avocados said RIPE-ish.

Denise wiped her fingers on a receipt.

“I’m leaving,” she said. “I’m never leaving. I’ve booked the train.”

“To where?”

“Here,” she said. “Obviously not here.”

A gull landed near our feet, though we were miles from the sea. It had the self-possession of a landlord. Denise looked at it, and it looked back, and for a moment the three of us were arranged in a silence that felt almost planned.

Then Denise said, “Do you think cornflakes know they’re breakfast?”

The gull opened its beak and made no sound.

The rain began again, very lightly, like someone testing a sprinkler in the sky. It freckled the paper case in Denise’s palm. It darkened the shoulders of her coat. Across the park, the boys had stopped kicking the flat ball and were using it as a hat. The dachshund had got inside the crisp packet and was moving blindly among the leaves, silver-headed, ceremonial.

Denise stood.

“I’m completely happy,” she said, with her face arranged otherwise. “This is unbearable. Shall we look in the shops?”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem about a day out with a friend who makes strange pronouncements about men, Jesus, hell, and knowing her place, while the narrator notices ducks, crocuses, bicycles, and sunlight.
counterfactuals.output:
We walked where the path loosened  
beside the pond,  
spring pretending it had always been here.

Ducks stitched their green heads  
through the glittering water,  
important and ridiculous,  
as if the whole afternoon  
had been arranged for them.

You said, suddenly,  
men are made of doors  
and only some of them open.

Then you laughed  
like you had dropped a coin  
down a well.

Crocuses pressed up through the cold grass,  
purple mouths full of sun.  
A bicycle leaned against a railing,  
one wheel slowly turning  
though no one had touched it.

You said Jesus would understand  
about bad coffee,  
about the bus being late,  
about the way people look away  
when they have already decided  
who you are.

The light moved over your face  
in gold squares,  
through the branches,  
through the day’s thin mercy.

You said hell is probably  
just a room where everyone  
keeps explaining themselves  
and no one ever listens.

A child in a red helmet  
wobbled past us,  
serious with effort.  
The ducks rose all at once,  
water breaking open beneath them.

Then, softer,  
as if quoting someone  
who still lived in your bones,  
you said a woman should know her place.

And I looked at the crocuses,  
their small bright refusal  
to stay underground,

looked at the bicycles flashing by,  
the spokes catching fire  
in the late sun,

looked at you  
standing in the path  
with your coat unbuttoned,  
your hair blown wild,  
your shadow reaching everywhere.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental short prose piece with run-on lyric sentences, closely observed urban details, and dialogue fragments, where the speaker recounts what “she said” during a walk through a park and town.
counterfactuals.output:
She said the pigeons looked like old men in borrowed coats and then she said no, like bank clerks after rain, and we were walking under the plane trees where the bark peeled in army colors and the path had gone soft with last night’s weather and a boy on a scooter skimmed past us saying sorry without turning his head, sorry like a bell, sorry like a stone thrown over his shoulder, and she said people in this town apologized the way they breathed, accidentally, only when leaving.

She said look at that, and I looked, because she said it as if the world had put down its name in wet cement, and there was a glove on the bench, black leather, palm up, collecting drops from the sycamore leaves, a small defeated animal, a hand without its person, and behind it the duck pond was green at the edges and silver in the middle where the wind kept worrying it, and a man in a nylon jacket was feeding bread to birds beneath the sign that said DO NOT FEED THE BIRDS, and she said signs were mostly prayers nobody meant to answer.

You laughed, I said.

Did I, she said.

You did.

Maybe I was coughing, she said, and then she smiled in the direction of the bandstand where no band had played for years, only teenagers in the evenings, only cans rolling under the railings, only the municipal brass of rainwater and skateboard wheels, and she said when she was little she thought towns had secrets they hid in their parks, not bodies exactly, though sometimes bodies, but promises, lost teeth, folded notes, the names of those who had sat on benches and decided not to go home.

We came out by the iron gates where the paint had bubbled and flaked, and the traffic was waiting beyond them with its bright impatience, buses sighing, taxis nosing forward, a cyclist cursing into the wet air, the florist shaking buckets onto the pavement so the water ran pink and green around our shoes, and she said the high street always smelled like three things at once, lilies, diesel, and frying oil, which was how you knew you were alive but not necessarily well, and from the bakery came a heat so sweet it seemed to touch our faces with both hands.

She said, I should buy bread.

You don’t need bread, I said.

That has never stopped anyone, she said.

Inside the window the loaves were sleeping under flour, the cakes had red cherries fixed in their centers like little warning lights, and the girl behind the counter was laughing into her phone with one blue glove on and one blue glove off, the naked hand arranging change, the gloved hand lifting buns, and she said there were whole philosophies in how people touched money and food, and then she said no, forget I said that, I sound unbearable, and a delivery van reversed with its open-mouthed beeping and a woman dragging a shopping trolley shouted wait, wait, though nobody knew who she meant.

At the crossing the green man blinked us forward and she stepped before I did, always stepping before I did, her coat loose at the hem, one button missing, the scarf at her throat printed with tiny yellow birds, and she said she liked the exact middle of the road because for two seconds nobody owned you, not the shops, not the park, not the office windows, not the flats above the nail salon with their damp curtains and potted basil and satellite dishes angled toward weather or heaven, and a bus passed so close the advertisement on its side became a moving wall of teeth and perfume and impossible skin.

She said, do you ever think we are being followed by our younger selves.

I said, not followed.

Haunted then.

Accompanied, I said.

She said that was a kinder word and therefore less likely to be true.

Past the charity shop, where the mannequins wore sequins at ten in the morning and one had no head but a necklace anyway, past the betting shop with its door propped open and its blue screens glowing like aquariums of bad luck, past the closed cinema with the poster frames empty and the ticket booth dusty as an old eye, she kept talking or not talking, which with her had never been opposites, and she said the town had changed and not changed, the phone repair place used to be a butcher, the butcher used to be a travel agent, the travel agent used to have posters of beaches so bright you could feel your life accusing you from the window.

A dog barked from the upstairs of a house we could not see.

She said, there, even the invisible are asking to be let out.

I wanted to write that down, but I did not, because when you write something down too quickly it stops belonging to the air that made it, and she was still speaking, or the town was speaking through her, coins in a cup, gulls tearing open a bin bag, the church clock giving the wrong hour with confidence, a pram wheel catching in a crack, schoolchildren loosening their ties as if escaping small polite nooses, the smell of weed in the alley behind the chemist, the chemist window full of beige elastic supports for knees, wrists, backs, all the future failures of the body arranged with prices.

She said, don’t look so sad.

I said, I’m not.

You look like a man listening to a song he won’t admit he knows.

And then the rain began again, thin at first, needling the dust from the awnings, stippling the canal-black gutters, making everyone briefly honest under their hoods and newspapers and raised shoulders, and we turned back toward the park because the town had reached its end or we had, and she said she liked the rain for giving surfaces something to confess, brick darkening, metal shining, leaves opening their little hands, and the glove on the bench, when we passed it again, had filled with water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic monologue describing a cold sunny day in the UK: tea in a café, Wilko’s purchases, a library in a park, Butterworth’s bikes, and a companion whose comments reveal trauma, religion, and internalized misogyny.
counterfactuals.output:
The sun is out, but it has no heat in it—  
only that pale English brightness  
that lays a silver blade along the pavements  
and makes every window in town look briefly holy.

We sit in the café with our coats still on,  
hands wrapped around mugs of tea  
as if the china were a small domestic fire.  
Outside, buses hiss at the kerb,  
schoolchildren scatter like starlings,  
and the sky is a hard, rinsed blue  
over rooftops blackened by old rain.

You stir and stir, though you take no sugar.  
The spoon rings softly against the cup,  
a little bell calling no one.

I have a Wilko bag tucked beneath the chair—  
washing-up sponges, a packet of batteries,  
cheap notebooks, a tin of gloss paint  
whose colour promised “Warm Ivory”  
under fluorescent light.  
Ordinary things.  
The kind of purchases that say  
a life can be mended in small ways:  
a loose drawer, a dead torch,  
a room made brighter by degrees.

You laugh at that, but not kindly.  
“Women always think a clean house can save them,”  
you say, and then look out of the window  
as if the sentence had been placed in your mouth  
by someone standing behind you.  
I see him there for a moment—  
not a man exactly, but a weather system:  
the father, the preacher, the old boyfriend,  
the voice that taught you  
a girl’s body was a locked church  
and shame the only key.

You speak of God as if He were a landlord,  
always inspecting, always disappointed.  
You say forgiveness is a duty,  
that suffering makes people pure,  
that good women endure.  
Then your eyes go flat  
and young  
and far away.

The day keeps shining brutally.

After tea we walk through the park  
towards the library,  
that red-brick ark of municipal mercy  
set among winter trees.  
The grass is stiff with frost  
where the sun has not reached,  
and pigeons step about importantly  
like clerks in grey waistcoats.  
Inside, the library smells of paper, radiator dust,  
and rain dried from wool.  
It is warm enough to make us drowsy.  
Children whisper too loudly.  
An old man reads the racing pages.  
A woman in the crime aisle runs her fingers  
along the spines  
as though choosing which darkness  
she can bear today.

You pause by the theology shelf  
and say, “They never tell girls  
how much of faith is just fear  
with flowers round it.”

Then, almost at once:  
“But modesty matters.  
Women bring trouble on themselves.”  
Your voice tightens around the words  
like a hand closing.  
I want to take them from you,  
these rusted tools you were given  
and told were wisdom.  
I want to say:  
No. No, beloved.  
That was not God.  
That was not love.  
That was someone teaching you  
to kneel before the wound  
and call it an altar.

But the librarian stamps a book,  
the clock ticks,  
the sun pours cold gold  
through the high windows,  
and I say only,  
“Come on. Let’s keep walking.”

Past Butterworth’s Bikes,  
where the bicycles hang in the window  
sleek as bright animals—  
red frames, blue frames,  
silver spokes catching the afternoon  
and breaking it into sparks.  
You stand before them longer than expected.  
For once you say nothing about sin  
or duty  
or what women are made for.  
You say, quietly,  
“I used to want one like that.  
I used to think I could just ride away.”

And there it is—  
the whole country holding its breath:  
the cold sun, the tea cooling in memory,  
the Wilko bag knocking against my knee,  
the library warm in the park behind us,  
the bicycles waiting like possible futures.

I look at you,  
your face bright on one side, shadowed on the other,  
and I think how people survive  
by speaking in broken scriptures,  
by mistaking cages for commandments,  
by calling the bars protection  
until some winter afternoon  
when light falls cleanly on the lock.

The day is freezing.  
The day is full of sun.  
And somewhere inside you,  
beneath all that inherited thunder,  
a wheel is turning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
